quilter-the-bracelet.music: Graceful and light, in the old style of Herrick's verse.

quilter-the-maiden-blush.written: Composed and published in 1905 (Op. 8), for the tenor Gervase Elwes
quilter-the-maiden-blush.story: As cherries blush and roses, so Julia blushes: the poet lists the loveliest pinks and reds in nature to describe her face.
quilter-the-maiden-blush.poem: Words by Robert Herrick (1591-1674), from Hesperides (1648).

quilter-to-daisies.written: Composed and published in 1905 (Op. 8), for the tenor Gervase Elwes
quilter-to-daisies.story: Do not close yet, daisies, though the evening comes: wait until Julia goes to sleep, then shut your eyes too.
quilter-to-daisies.poem: Words by Robert Herrick (1591-1674), from Hesperides (1648).
quilter-to-daisies.music: Slow and lulling, almost a lullaby.

quilter-the-night-piece.written: Composed and published in 1905 (Op. 8), for the tenor Gervase Elwes
quilter-the-night-piece.story: Let the glow-worm lend you its eyes, and the stars light your way to me, Julia, through the night; no will-o'-the-wisp will lead you astray.
quilter-the-night-piece.poem: Words by Robert Herrick (1591-1674), from Hesperides (1648).
quilter-the-night-piece.music: Mysterious and nocturnal, with soft, glimmering figures in the piano.

quilter-julias-hair.written: Composed and published in 1905 (Op. 8), for the tenor Gervase Elwes
quilter-julias-hair.story: Julia's hair, scattered by the wind, is like a net, a sea of gold: the poet is caught in it.
quilter-julias-hair.poem: Words by Robert Herrick (1591-1674), from Hesperides (1648).

quilter-cherry-ripe.written: Composed and published in 1905 (Op. 8), for the tenor Gervase Elwes
quilter-cherry-ripe.story: Cherry ripe, ripe, ripe, I cry: come buy. Where do the cherries grow? On Julia's lips, there where the cherries grow.
quilter-cherry-ripe.poem: Words by Robert Herrick (1591-1674), from Hesperides (1648).
quilter-cherry-ripe.music: A street seller's cry turned into a quick, sparkling song that ends the cycle brightly.

somervell-loveliest-of-trees-the-cherry-.story: At Eastertide the cherry is hung with white blossom. He is twenty; fifty springs are little room to see things in bloom, so he will go out to see the cherry hung with snow.
somervell-loveliest-of-trees-the-cherry-.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-loveliest-of-trees-the-cherry-.music: A gentle, flowing opening to the cycle. Compare it with Butterworth's darker setting of the same poem.

somervell-when-i-was-one-and-twenty.story: When he was one-and-twenty a wise man told him: give away your money, but not your heart. He did not listen; now he is two-and-twenty, and it is true.
somervell-when-i-was-one-and-twenty.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-when-i-was-one-and-twenty.music: Light and wry, two verses, with a sigh at the end.

somervell-there-pass-the-careless-people.story: The careless people pass by, calling their souls their own; he stands apart, thinking of a lover who has left him.
somervell-there-pass-the-careless-people.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).

somervell-in-summer-time-on-bredon.story: In summer on Bredon hill the church bells ring and the lovers lie listening. They will be married, he says; but in winter she goes to church alone, to her funeral, and now he says to the bells: I hear you, I will come.
somervell-in-summer-time-on-bredon.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-in-summer-time-on-bredon.music: The bells are in the piano; the mood turns from summer happiness to winter grief.

somervell-the-street-sounds-to-the-soldi.story: The street rings with the soldiers' tread; the lad watches them march by and wishes them well, knowing many will not come back.
somervell-the-street-sounds-to-the-soldi.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-the-street-sounds-to-the-soldi.music: A march rhythm in the piano.

somervell-on-the-idle-hill-of-summer.story: Lying sleepy on a summer hill, he hears far off the drums and fifes of soldiers marching to die. Woman bore me, he says; I will rise and go.
somervell-on-the-idle-hill-of-summer.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-on-the-idle-hill-of-summer.music: Drowsy at first, then the distant drum comes nearer.

somervell-white-in-the-moon-the-long-roa.story: White in the moonlight lies the long road that leads him away from his love; he walks on, knowing that the road goes round the world and will bring him back.
somervell-white-in-the-moon-the-long-roa.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-white-in-the-moon-the-long-roa.music: A walking rhythm and a long, sad line.

somervell-think-no-more-lad-laugh-be-jol.story: Think no more, lad: laugh, be jolly; thought is what spoils young men's lives. Drink, dance, and leave thinking to old age.
somervell-think-no-more-lad-laugh-be-jol.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-think-no-more-lad-laugh-be-jol.music: Quick and forced in its cheer.

somervell-into-my-heart-an-air-that-kill.story: An air from a far country blows into his heart: what are those blue remembered hills? It is the land of lost content, the happy highways where he went and cannot come again.
somervell-into-my-heart-an-air-that-kill.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-into-my-heart-an-air-that-kill.music: Very short and quiet; the most famous poem of the book.

somervell-the-lads-in-their-hundreds.story: The lads come in their hundreds to Ludlow fair. Many of them will never grow old, and no one can tell which: they will carry their good looks to the grave.
somervell-the-lads-in-their-hundreds.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), from A Shropshire Lad (1896).
somervell-the-lads-in-their-hundreds.music: A lilting fair-day tune darkened by the poem's knowledge.

gounod-le-premier-jour-de-mai.written: Composed between 1842 and 1850; published in 1855 in Six mélodies
gounod-le-premier-jour-de-mai.story: On the first day of May the poet greets his love with the spring, hoping she will be as gentle as the season.
gounod-le-premier-jour-de-mai.music: Graceful and bright, in the manner of an old French song.

gounod-o-ma-belle-rebelle.written: Composed between 1842 and 1850; published in 1855 in Six mélodies
gounod-o-ma-belle-rebelle.story: O my lovely rebel, so harsh to me: will you never let me kiss your eyes and lips? Your cruelty is killing me.
gounod-o-ma-belle-rebelle.music: Tender and pleading, with a lute-like accompaniment.

gounod-aubade.written: Composed between 1842 and 1850; published in 1855 in Six mélodies
gounod-aubade.story: A morning song: the lover sings to his beloved at dawn, calling her to wake.
gounod-aubade.music: Light and fresh, with a serenading accompaniment.

gounod-le-lever.written: Composed between 1842 and 1850; published in 1855 in Six mélodies
gounod-le-lever.story: Enough sleep, my beauty: dawn is breaking, the horses are ready; come, let us ride out together into the morning.
gounod-le-lever.music: Brisk and lively, with a galloping rhythm.

gounod-venise.written: Composed between 1842 and 1850; published in 1855 in Six mélodies
gounod-venise.story: Night in Venice: not a gondola moving, the lions of St Mark asleep, the lovers at their windows; the poet invites his beloved to the hour of love.
gounod-venise.music: A lilting barcarolle, the gondola's rocking in the piano.

gounod-le-soir.written: Composed around 1840-42 (CG 441); published in 1863 in Gounod's 20 Mélodies
gounod-le-soir.story: Evening falls; the poet sits alone in the twilight and watches the first star. A ray of moonlight seems to carry the soul of someone he loved and lost.
gounod-le-soir.poem: Words by Alphonse de Lamartine (1790-1869), from his Méditations poétiques (1820).
gounod-le-soir.music: Gounod wrote it during his years in Rome: slow, warm and calm.

schumann-aus-meinen-tranen-spriessen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-aus-meinen-tranen-spriessen.story: From his tears spring many blooming flowers, and his sighs become a choir of nightingales. If she loves him, he will give her all the flowers, and the nightingale will sing at her window.
schumann-aus-meinen-tranen-spriessen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-aus-meinen-tranen-spriessen.music: Very short and simple, almost a continuation of the first song.

schumann-die-rose-die-lilie.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-die-rose-die-lilie.story: The rose, the lily, the dove, the sun: he loved them all once. Now he loves only her, the little, the fine, the pure, the one.
schumann-die-rose-die-lilie.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-die-rose-die-lilie.music: A quick, breathless patter: the whole song lasts about thirty seconds.

schumann-wenn-ich-in-deine-augen-seh.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-wenn-ich-in-deine-augen-seh.story: When he looks into her eyes all his pain vanishes; when he kisses her mouth he is healed. But when she says 'I love you', he must weep bitterly.
schumann-wenn-ich-in-deine-augen-seh.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-wenn-ich-in-deine-augen-seh.music: Slow and tender; the last line, 'so muss ich weinen bitterlich', is the heart of it.

schumann-ich-will-meine-seele-tauchen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-ich-will-meine-seele-tauchen.story: He wants to dip his soul into the cup of a lily, so that it breathes a song of his beloved, a song that trembles like the kiss she once gave him.
schumann-ich-will-meine-seele-tauchen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-ich-will-meine-seele-tauchen.music: Rippling arpeggios like a breath of air; quiet and quick.

schumann-und-wusstens-die-blumen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-und-wusstens-die-blumen.story: If the flowers knew how deeply he is wounded, they would weep with him; the nightingales and the stars would comfort him. But they cannot know: only she knows, and she has torn his heart.
schumann-und-wusstens-die-blumen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-und-wusstens-die-blumen.music: Restless, fluttering accompaniment, and a violent piano postlude.

schumann-das-ist-ein-floten-und-geigen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-das-ist-ein-floten-und-geigen.story: Flutes and violins, trumpets blaring: it is her wedding dance, and the angels are sobbing.
schumann-das-ist-ein-floten-und-geigen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-das-ist-ein-floten-und-geigen.music: The piano plays a whirling waltz throughout; the voice weaves in and out of it. A famous piano part.

schumann-hor-ich-das-liedchen-klingen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-hor-ich-das-liedchen-klingen.story: When he hears the little song she used to sing, his heart nearly bursts; he goes up to the woods to weep out his grief.
schumann-hor-ich-das-liedchen-klingen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-hor-ich-das-liedchen-klingen.music: Slow, aching and simple, with a long, sad piano postlude.

schumann-ein-jungling-liebt-ein-madchen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-ein-jungling-liebt-ein-madchen.story: A young man loves a girl who loves another; that one loves another girl and marries her. It is an old story, yet always new, and whoever it happens to, it breaks his heart.
schumann-ein-jungling-liebt-ein-madchen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-ein-jungling-liebt-ein-madchen.music: A jaunty, almost mocking tune that hides the bitterness.

schumann-am-leuchtenden-sommermorgen.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-am-leuchtenden-sommermorgen.story: On a bright summer morning he walks in the garden. The flowers whisper to him: do not be angry with our sister, you sad, pale man.
schumann-am-leuchtenden-sommermorgen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-am-leuchtenden-sommermorgen.music: Gentle arpeggios and a still, floating line; the piano's postlude is famous.

schumann-ich-hab-im-traum-geweinet.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-ich-hab-im-traum-geweinet.story: He wept in a dream that she lay in her grave; he dreamt she had left him; he dreamt she loved him still, and he is still weeping.
schumann-ich-hab-im-traum-geweinet.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-ich-hab-im-traum-geweinet.music: Voice and piano alternate in silence-filled phrases: some of the starkest bars Schumann wrote.

schumann-allnachtlich-im-traume.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-allnachtlich-im-traume.story: Every night in dreams he sees her; she greets him kindly, gives him a sprig of cypress, and whispers a word. When he wakes, the cypress is gone and he has forgotten the word.
schumann-allnachtlich-im-traume.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-allnachtlich-im-traume.music: Short, hesitant phrases with pauses; a dream half remembered.

schumann-aus-alten-marchen-winkt-es.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-aus-alten-marchen-winkt-es.story: From old fairy tales a magic land beckons, with flowers in golden evening light and singing trees; if only he could go there and be happy. But the vision melts away like foam.
schumann-aus-alten-marchen-winkt-es.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-aus-alten-marchen-winkt-es.music: Bright and lively, the longest of the fantasy songs, ending in sudden sadness.

schumann-die-alten-bosen-lieder.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48); published in 1844 in Dichterliebe
schumann-die-alten-bosen-lieder.story: The old, bitter songs and dreams: he will bury them in a huge coffin, carried by twelve giants and sunk in the sea. Do you know why the coffin must be so heavy? He is burying his love and his pain in it.
schumann-die-alten-bosen-lieder.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-die-alten-bosen-lieder.music: Heavy and grand, then a tender piano postlude that remembers the twelfth song: the last word of the cycle is the piano's.

schumann-er-der-herrlichste-von-allen.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-er-der-herrlichste-von-allen.story: He, the most wonderful of all, so gentle and good: she sees him far above her, like a star, and wishes him the worthiest of brides, even if her heart breaks.
schumann-er-der-herrlichste-von-allen.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-er-der-herrlichste-von-allen.music: Fast, ardent and full of admiration.

schumann-ich-kanns-nicht-fassen.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-ich-kanns-nicht-fassen.story: She cannot believe it: he has chosen her. It must be a dream; she wants to die in that dream, drowned in endless joy.
schumann-ich-kanns-nicht-fassen.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-ich-kanns-nicht-fassen.music: Breathless and excited, with outbursts of disbelief.

schumann-helft-mir-ihr-schwestern.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-helft-mir-ihr-schwestern.story: Help me, sisters, to dress for my wedding: put on the myrtles. She greets her sisters with joy and a touch of sadness as she leaves them.
schumann-helft-mir-ihr-schwestern.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-helft-mir-ihr-schwestern.music: A bright, busy wedding song that ends in a wedding march.

schumann-susser-freund-du-blickest.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-susser-freund-du-blickest.story: Dear friend, you look at me in wonder; come close, let me whisper in your ear why I am crying. She is expecting their child.
schumann-susser-freund-du-blickest.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-susser-freund-du-blickest.music: Slow, intimate and hushed: the turning point of the cycle.

schumann-an-meinem-herzen.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-an-meinem-herzen.story: At my heart, at my breast: the young mother sings of her happiness with her baby; only a mother knows what it is to love.
schumann-an-meinem-herzen.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-an-meinem-herzen.music: Quick and jubilant, almost bursting with joy.

schumann-nun-hast-du-mir-den-ersten-schm.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42); published in 1843 in Frauenliebe und -leben
schumann-nun-hast-du-mir-den-ersten-schm.story: Now you have caused me my first pain: you sleep, hard and pitiless man, the sleep of death. She withdraws into herself, to her memories of him.
schumann-nun-hast-du-mir-den-ersten-schm.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-nun-hast-du-mir-den-ersten-schm.music: Stark recitative-like phrases; then the long piano postlude brings back the music of the first song, as a memory.

schubert-halt.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-halt.story: The miller sees a mill among the alders and hears the wheels: is this where the brook was leading him?
schubert-halt.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-halt.music: The piano's turning figures are the mill wheels.

schubert-danksagung-an-den-bach.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-danksagung-an-den-bach.story: Was this what you meant, my brook? Did she send you? He thanks the brook for bringing him here.
schubert-danksagung-an-den-bach.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-danksagung-an-den-bach.music: Gentle and grateful, flowing like the water.

schubert-am-feierabend.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-am-feierabend.story: If he had a thousand arms he would work so hard the miller's daughter would notice him. But at the end of the day she says goodnight to all the lads alike.
schubert-am-feierabend.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-am-feierabend.music: Busy, energetic piano for the work; then a quieter, disappointed close.

schubert-der-neugierige.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-der-neugierige.story: He asks the brook, not the flowers or stars: does she love me? Yes or no, two little words.
schubert-der-neugierige.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-der-neugierige.music: Tender and questioning, with a beautiful hush on 'ja' and 'nein'.

schubert-ungeduld.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-ungeduld.story: He wants to carve it into every tree, write it on every stone: dein ist mein Herz, my heart is yours and shall be for ever.
schubert-ungeduld.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-ungeduld.music: Fast and impatient, each verse ending in an outburst; strophic.

schubert-morgengruss.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-morgengruss.story: Good morning, lovely miller's girl: why do you turn away? He will stand far off and only look at your window.
schubert-morgengruss.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-morgengruss.music: A gentle, swaying morning greeting; strophic.

schubert-des-mullers-blumen.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-des-mullers-blumen.story: Blue flowers grow by the brook, the colour of her eyes. He plants them under her window to whisper to her of him in her dreams.
schubert-des-mullers-blumen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).

schubert-tranenregen.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-tranenregen.story: They sit together by the brook in the moonlight and look into the water. Tears fill his eyes; she says it is going to rain, and goes home.
schubert-tranenregen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-tranenregen.music: A calm, tender song with a sudden chill at the end.

schubert-mein.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-mein.story: Mine! He wants the whole world to hear it: the beloved miller's girl is mine.
schubert-mein.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-mein.music: Exuberant and fast, the high point of his happiness.

schubert-pause.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-pause.story: He has hung his lute on the wall, wrapped in a green ribbon: his heart is too full to sing.
schubert-pause.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-pause.music: Quiet and hesitant, the piano plucking like the lute.

schubert-mit-dem-grunen-lautenbande.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-mit-dem-grunen-lautenbande.story: She likes green so much; he gives her the green ribbon from his lute for her hair. Green is the colour of hope.
schubert-mit-dem-grunen-lautenbande.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).

schubert-der-jager.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-der-jager.story: What is the hunter doing here by the mill stream? He should go back to his forest; let him shoot the boars that dig up her cabbage instead.
schubert-der-jager.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-der-jager.music: Fast and agitated, with hunting-horn figures.

schubert-eifersucht-und-stolz.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-eifersucht-und-stolz.story: Where are you rushing, brook? After the hunter? Go and tell her that he, the miller, is playing happily, not crying.
schubert-eifersucht-und-stolz.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-eifersucht-und-stolz.music: Rushing and furious, the brook in the piano racing on.

schubert-die-liebe-farbe.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-die-liebe-farbe.story: He will dress in green, the colour of weeping willow and cypress; his love loves green, the hunter's colour.
schubert-die-liebe-farbe.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-die-liebe-farbe.music: A single repeated note tolls in the piano throughout, like a bell.

schubert-die-bose-farbe.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-die-bose-farbe.story: He would like to go out into the wide world, if only it were not so green. He hates the colour now: it is the hunter's.
schubert-die-bose-farbe.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-die-bose-farbe.music: Violent and bitter, with hunting horns turning sinister.

schubert-trockne-blumen.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-trockne-blumen.story: The flowers she gave him will lie with him in his grave. When she walks past and thinks: he was true, then spring will come again.
schubert-trockne-blumen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-trockne-blumen.music: A slow, desolate song that turns briefly to major at the dream of spring.

schubert-der-muller-und-der-bach.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-der-muller-und-der-bach.story: The miller and the brook talk: where a true heart dies of love, the lilies wilt. The brook promises rest; the miller lies down in it.
schubert-der-muller-und-der-bach.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-der-muller-und-der-bach.music: A dialogue: the miller in minor, the brook answering in major.

schumann-in-der-fremde-i.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-in-der-fremde-i.story: Far from home, behind the red lightning, the clouds come from his homeland; but his father and mother are long dead and no one knows him there. Soon he too will rest, and the forest will rustle over him.
schumann-in-der-fremde-i.music: Rippling guitar-like arpeggios and a still, melancholy line.

schumann-intermezzo.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-intermezzo.story: He carries her image deep in his heart; it looks at him so freshly and gladly. His heart sings an old, beautiful song that flies to her.
schumann-intermezzo.music: Syncopated, breathless accompaniment and a warm melody.

schumann-die-stille.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-die-stille.story: No one knows how happy he is: only one person knows. He wishes he were a bird, flying over the sea to heaven.

schumann-schone-fremde.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-schone-fremde.story: The treetops rustle and shudder as if the old gods were walking around. In the moonlight the night speaks of a great happiness to come.
schumann-schone-fremde.music: Rustling, excited accompaniment and an ecstatic climax.

schumann-auf-einer-burg.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-auf-einer-burg.story: An old knight sits asleep on watch in a ruined castle, turned to stone. Below on the Rhine a wedding party sails by, and the beautiful bride is weeping.
schumann-auf-einer-burg.music: Archaic, slow counterpoint like old church music; it ends unresolved.

schumann-in-der-fremde-ii.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-in-der-fremde-ii.story: He hears the brooks and doesn't know where he is; a nightingale sings as if of old times. It is as though his love were waiting in the old castle; but she died long ago.
schumann-in-der-fremde-ii.music: Restless, flowing accompaniment and a mood between dream and grief.

schumann-wehmuth.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-wehmuth.story: He can sing as if he were happy, but tears flow in secret. So nightingales sing out of their cage, and people rejoice, not knowing the pain in the song.
schumann-wehmuth.music: A slow, simple melody over gentle chords.

schumann-zwielicht.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39); published in 1842 in the Liederkreis
schumann-zwielicht.story: Twilight spreads its wings; trees shudder. Beware: if you have a deer you love, do not let it graze alone; trust no friend in this hour. Something goes lost in the night: be watchful.
schumann-zwielicht.music: Eerie, chromatic counterpoint in the piano; one of Schumann's darkest songs.

schumann-freisinn.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-freisinn.story: Let me sit in my saddle; you stay in your houses and tents. I ride freely into the distance, and over my cap there are only stars.
schumann-freisinn.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, from his West-östlicher Divan (1819).
schumann-freisinn.music: Brisk and proud, a riding rhythm.

schumann-jemand.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-jemand.story: My heart is sad, and I cannot tell you why: it is for someone. I would do anything for someone, keep someone safe.
schumann-jemand.poem: Words by Robert Burns ('For the sake o' Somebody'), in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.
schumann-jemand.music: A tender, folk-like song with a gentle lilt.

schumann-sitz-ich-allein.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-sitz-ich-allein.story: When I sit alone, where better than with myself? I drink my wine alone; no one stops me, and I have my own thoughts.
schumann-sitz-ich-allein.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, from the West-östlicher Divan.

schumann-setze-mir-nicht.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-setze-mir-nicht.story: Don't bang the jug down in front of me, you lout; whoever brings me wine should look friendly, or the wine goes sour.
schumann-setze-mir-nicht.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, from the West-östlicher Divan.

schumann-talismane.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-talismane.story: God's is the Orient, God's is the Occident; north and south rest peacefully in his hands. He, the only just one, wants what is right for all.
schumann-talismane.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, from the West-östlicher Divan.
schumann-talismane.music: A grand, contrapuntal hymn; the 'Amen' is set in fugal style.

schumann-lied-der-suleika.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-lied-der-suleika.story: How well I understand your wishes, beloved: you long to be near me, as I long for you.
schumann-lied-der-suleika.poem: Words by Marianne von Willemer, published by Goethe as his own in the West-östlicher Divan.

schumann-die-hochlander-witwe.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-die-hochlander-witwe.story: A Highland widow laments: she once had cattle and sheep and a husband; all was lost when he fell in battle.
schumann-die-hochlander-witwe.poem: Words by Robert Burns ('The Highland Widow's Lament'), in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.
schumann-die-hochlander-witwe.music: Fast and agitated, full of grief and anger.

schumann-lieder-der-braut-ii-lass-mich-i.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-lieder-der-braut-ii-lass-mich-i.story: Let me hang on his breast, mother, let me stay; she has found her place with her bridegroom.
schumann-lieder-der-braut-ii-lass-mich-i.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert, from his Liebesfrühling.

schumann-hochlandisches-wiegenlied.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-hochlandisches-wiegenlied.story: Sleep, little child: your father is a Highlander, a brave man, and you will be one too.
schumann-hochlandisches-wiegenlied.poem: Words by Robert Burns, in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.

schumann-aus-den-hebraischen-gesangen-me.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-aus-den-hebraischen-gesangen-me.story: My heart is heavy: strike the harp, let its notes break through the darkness, or my heart will burst.
schumann-aus-den-hebraischen-gesangen-me.poem: Words by Lord Byron ('My Soul is Dark', from Hebrew Melodies, 1815), in Karl Julius Körner's German translation.
schumann-aus-den-hebraischen-gesangen-me.music: Dark and heavy, with a harp-like middle section.

schumann-ratsel.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-ratsel.story: A riddle: what is whispered in heaven and muttered in hell, found in a sigh but lost in a whisper? The letter H.
schumann-ratsel.poem: Words by Catherine Maria Fanshawe (1765-1834), in German translation.

schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-i-lei.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-i-lei.story: Row gently, gondolier, to her window; let no one hear us glide through the night to my love.
schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-i-lei.poem: Words by Thomas Moore, in Ferdinand Freiligrath's German translation.

schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-ii-we.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-ii-we.story: When the evening breeze moves over the Piazza, come, masked, to meet me; I will know you by the sign we agreed.
schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-ii-we.poem: Words by Thomas Moore, in Ferdinand Freiligrath's German translation.
schumann-zwei-venetianische-lieder-ii-we.music: Quick and conspiratorial, a Venetian carnival scene.

schumann-hauptmanns-weib.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-hauptmanns-weib.story: The captain's wife rides with her husband to war; wherever he goes, she goes too.
schumann-hauptmanns-weib.poem: Words by Robert Burns, in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.

schumann-was-will-die-einsame-trane.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-was-will-die-einsame-trane.story: What does this lonely tear want? It is left over from long ago; the others have all flowed away. It too should melt away now.
schumann-was-will-die-einsame-trane.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).

schumann-niemand.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-niemand.story: I have a wife of my own; I'll share her with nobody. I'll take no one's cuckold's horns, and give none.
schumann-niemand.poem: Words by Robert Burns ('I hae a wife o' my ain'), in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.

schumann-im-westen.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-im-westen.story: He looks out over the sea to the west, where his love is; the wind carries his longing to her.
schumann-im-westen.poem: Words by Robert Burns, in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.

schumann-du-bist-wie-eine-blume.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-du-bist-wie-eine-blume.story: You are like a flower, so sweet and pure; looking at you, sadness creeps into my heart. I want to lay my hands on your head and pray God keeps you so.
schumann-du-bist-wie-eine-blume.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-du-bist-wie-eine-blume.music: Very short, with soft repeated chords; one of Schumann's most famous songs.

schumann-aus-den-ostlichen-rosen.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-aus-den-ostlichen-rosen.story: A greeting from the eastern roses: wherever you are, may their scent reach you.
schumann-aus-den-ostlichen-rosen.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert, from Östliche Rosen (1822).

schumann-zum-schluss.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-zum-schluss.story: To end: here I have woven you a wreath, imperfect as it is; in heaven it will be made whole.
schumann-zum-schluss.music: A quiet, devoted ending to the book.

schubert-liebesbotschaft.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-liebesbotschaft.story: Rushing brook, so silver bright: hurry to my beloved, bring her my greeting, refresh her flowers, and sing her to sleep.
schubert-liebesbotschaft.music: The piano's rippling figures are the brook, as in Die schöne Müllerin.

schubert-kriegers-ahnung.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-kriegers-ahnung.story: Soldiers sleep around the campfire; one keeps watch and thinks of his love, sensing he will not see her again.
schubert-kriegers-ahnung.music: A dark march, a tender memory, and a desperate climax.

schubert-aufenthalt.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-aufenthalt.story: Roaring river, rustling forest, towering rock: this is my resting place. As wave follows wave, so my tears flow.
schubert-aufenthalt.music: Powerful driving triplets; one of Schubert's most dramatic songs.

schubert-in-der-ferne.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-in-der-ferne.story: Woe to the one who flees, who leaves his mother's house behind and wanders in the world: no one blesses his road.
schubert-in-der-ferne.music: Bleak and slow, with strange harmonies.

schubert-abschied.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-abschied.story: Farewell, you merry town: the rider waves goodbye to everything, on his trotting horse, and rides away.
schubert-abschied.music: The piano trots throughout; cheerful and quick.

schubert-der-atlas.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-der-atlas.story: I, unhappy Atlas: I must carry a world, the whole world of sorrows. You proud heart, you wanted to be infinitely happy, or infinitely wretched: now you are wretched.
schubert-der-atlas.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schubert-der-atlas.music: Massive and defiant, with a tremolo bass; it needs power.

schubert-ihr-bild.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-ihr-bild.story: He stood in dark dreams gazing at her portrait, and her face seemed to come alive, to smile, with tears in her eyes. And I cannot believe that I have lost you.
schubert-ihr-bild.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schubert-ihr-bild.music: Very bare: voice and piano in octaves, with silences between.

schubert-das-fischermadchen.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-das-fischermadchen.story: Lovely fisher girl, bring your boat to land; sit with me and hold hands. My heart is like the sea, with storms and tides and many pearls in its depths.
schubert-das-fischermadchen.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).

schubert-die-stadt.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-die-stadt.story: At dusk the town appears on the horizon, wrapped in mist. The boatman rows; the sun rises once more and shows him the place where he lost his beloved.
schubert-die-stadt.music: Eerie arpeggios in the piano, like wind on water.

schubert-der-doppelganger.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-der-doppelganger.story: A quiet night in the empty street where his beloved used to live. A man stands there, staring up and wringing his hands in pain; the moon shows his face: it is his own.
schubert-der-doppelganger.music: Four slow chords repeated like a ground bass; the voice rises to a terrifying climax. One of the greatest songs ever written.

schubert-die-taubenpost.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-die-taubenpost.story: He has a carrier pigeon that flies to his beloved with his letters: her name is Longing.
schubert-die-taubenpost.music: Light and charming, Schubert's last song.

schubert-die-wetterfahne.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-die-wetterfahne.story: The wind plays with the weather vane on her house: he should have known by it that she was fickle. What do they care inside? Their daughter is a rich bride.
schubert-die-wetterfahne.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-die-wetterfahne.music: A sharp, gusting figure in the piano.

schubert-gefrorne-thranen.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-gefrorne-thranen.story: Frozen tears fall from his cheeks; he did not notice he was weeping. Tears, are you so lukewarm that you turn to ice?
schubert-gefrorne-thranen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-gefrorne-thranen.music: Slow, halting steps in the piano.

schubert-erstarrung.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-erstarrung.story: He searches the snow for her footprints, where they walked in the green meadow. He wants to melt the ice with his tears; his heart is frozen, her image frozen inside it.
schubert-erstarrung.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-erstarrung.music: Driving triplets and a restless line.

schubert-wasserfluth.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-wasserfluth.story: His tears fall into the snow; when the snow melts, it will flow with the brook through the town to her house.
schubert-wasserfluth.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-wasserfluth.music: Slow, heavy triplets; a long, sad line.

schubert-auf-dem-flusse.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-auf-dem-flusse.story: The rushing river is frozen over. He carves her name and the date into the ice: is my heart like this river under its crust, raging?
schubert-auf-dem-flusse.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-auf-dem-flusse.music: Quiet, frozen staccato that breaks into turmoil at the end.

schubert-ruckblick.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-ruckblick.story: He runs from the town as if pursued, remembering how it greeted him when he came: birds, lime trees, her eyes. He wishes he could go back and stand before her house.
schubert-ruckblick.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-ruckblick.music: Fast and agitated, then a gentle memory in major.

schubert-irrlicht.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-irrlicht.story: A will-o'-the-wisp lures him into the rocky depths; he does not mind. Every path leads to the goal; every river reaches the sea, every sorrow its grave.
schubert-irrlicht.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-rast.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-rast.story: Only now that he stops, in a charcoal burner's hut, does he feel how tired he is; and his heart, at rest, feels the worm inside it.
schubert-rast.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-rast.music: A trudging tread in the piano.

schubert-fruhlingstraum.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-fruhlingstraum.story: He dreamt of colourful flowers and green meadows; then the cocks crowed and he woke to cold darkness and frost flowers on the window.
schubert-fruhlingstraum.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-fruhlingstraum.music: Three moods: a sweet dream, a harsh awakening, and longing.

schubert-einsamkeit.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911); published in January 1828 in Winterreise, Part 1
schubert-einsamkeit.story: Like a dark cloud passing over the treetops, he goes his way alone. The air is calm, the world bright; he was happier when storms raged.
schubert-einsamkeit.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-einsamkeit.music: Slow walking steps, with a stormy outburst.

schubert-die-post.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-die-post.story: The post horn sounds in the street: why does my heart leap? There's no letter for you, my heart. Still you want to know how she is.
schubert-die-post.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-die-post.music: The post horn and the galloping horse in the piano.

schubert-der-greise-kopf.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-der-greise-kopf.story: Frost has made his hair white, and he rejoiced that he was old; but it melted. How far it is to the grave.
schubert-der-greise-kopf.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-die-krahe.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-die-krahe.story: A crow has followed him from the town, circling overhead. Will it wait for his body? Let me see loyalty unto the grave.
schubert-die-krahe.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-die-krahe.music: The piano's circling figure is the crow's flight.

schubert-letzte-hoffnung.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-letzte-hoffnung.story: He watches a leaf on a tree and hangs his hope on it. If the leaf falls, his hope falls with it, and he weeps on his hope's grave.
schubert-letzte-hoffnung.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-letzte-hoffnung.music: Fragmented, trembling rhythms like falling leaves.

schubert-im-dorfe.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-im-dorfe.story: In the village dogs bark, chains rattle; people sleep, dreaming of what they don't have. Bark me away, he tells the dogs: I'm done with dreams.
schubert-im-dorfe.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-im-dorfe.music: Growling bass trills and a quiet, bitter line.

schubert-der-sturmische-morgen.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-der-sturmische-morgen.story: A stormy morning has torn the sky's grey clothes; red flames dart between the clouds. That is a morning after my own heart: it is winter, cold and wild.
schubert-der-sturmische-morgen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-tauschung.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-tauschung.story: A light dances ahead of him; he follows it, knowing it is a trick. Only a wretch would let himself be lured by a bright, warm house and a loving soul.
schubert-tauschung.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-der-wegweiser.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-der-wegweiser.story: Why does he avoid the roads others take and seek hidden paths? One signpost stands unmoved before his eyes; he must take a road from which no one has returned.
schubert-der-wegweiser.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-der-wegweiser.music: A steady walking rhythm and a repeated note at the end, like a death knell.

schubert-das-wirthshaus.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-das-wirthshaus.story: His path leads to a graveyard: this is the inn he will stay at. But all the rooms are taken. Then onward, my faithful staff.
schubert-das-wirthshaus.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-muth.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-muth.story: When snow blows in his face he shakes it off; when his heart speaks, he sings loud and bright. If no god is on earth, we will be gods ourselves.
schubert-muth.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schubert-die-nebensonnen.written: Composed in October 1827 (D 911); published in December 1828 in Winterreise, Part 2
schubert-die-nebensonnen.story: He saw three suns in the sky. They are not his suns; he once had three, but the best two are gone. Let the third one go too; in the dark he will be better.
schubert-die-nebensonnen.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).

schumann-lieder-der-braut-i-mutter-mutte.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-lieder-der-braut-i-mutter-mutte.story: Mother, mother, do not think that because I love him I love you less. Ever since I have known him, I love you more: you gave me the heart that learned to love him.
schumann-lieder-der-braut-i-mutter-mutte.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert, from his Liebesfrühling.
schumann-lieder-der-braut-i-mutter-mutte.music: Tender and simple, a daughter's quiet reassurance.

mahler-ich-hab-ein-gluhend-messer.written: Composed in 1884-85; published in 1897 in Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen
mahler-ich-hab-ein-gluhend-messer.story: He has a glowing knife in his breast: it cuts into every joy. Day and night it gives him no rest. When he looks at the sky he sees her blue eyes; in the yellow fields, her blond hair blowing. He wishes he lay on the black bier, never to open his eyes again.
mahler-ich-hab-ein-gluhend-messer.poem: Words by Gustav Mahler, written after an unhappy love affair in Kassel.
mahler-ich-hab-ein-gluhend-messer.music: Wild and violent, with a raging accompaniment; the end collapses into a quiet, exhausted funeral tread.

schubert-am-meer.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-am-meer.story: The sea glittered in the last evening light; the lovers sat by a lonely fisherman's hut. She wept, and he knelt and drank the tears from her hand. Since that hour he has been wasting away: the unhappy woman has poisoned him with her tears.
schubert-am-meer.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Die Heimkehr in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schubert-am-meer.music: Opens and closes with the same mysterious two chords; the calm verses alternate with storms of tremolo in the piano.

schubert-des-baches-wiegenlied.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-des-baches-wiegenlied.story: The end of the cycle: the brook sings the drowned miller to sleep. Rest, weary wanderer, you are home; here is faithfulness. Sleep until the sea drinks up the brooks; the full moon rises, the mist parts, and the sky above is so wide.
schubert-des-baches-wiegenlied.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-des-baches-wiegenlied.music: A gentle, rocking lullaby in E major, five verses to the same music; it needs a perfectly steady, quiet line.

schubert-fruhlingssehnsucht.written: Composed in 1828 (D 957); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-fruhlingssehnsucht.story: Rustling breezes, brooks hurrying to the river, the gold of the sun: everything in spring draws towards love. Why does his heart alone stay restless? Only you can set free the spring in my heart.
schubert-fruhlingssehnsucht.music: Breathless and eager, with a question ('Wohin? Wohin?') at the end of each verse, and a rising passion through the five verses.

schumann-hochlanders-abschied.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-hochlanders-abschied.story: My heart's in the Highlands, my heart is not here; it is chasing the deer. Farewell to the mountains, the valleys, the torrents: wherever I wander, my heart is in the Highlands.
schumann-hochlanders-abschied.poem: Words by Robert Burns ('My Heart's in the Highlands'), in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.
schumann-hochlanders-abschied.music: A vigorous, swinging song with a horn-call rhythm in the piano.

schumann-weit-weit.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25); published in 1840 in Myrthen, Schumann's wedding gift to Clara
schumann-weit-weit.story: How can I be merry, how can I dance, when my love is far, far away? He gave me gloves, a coloured scarf and a silk dress; but what are they to me when he is far away?
schumann-weit-weit.poem: Words by Robert Burns ('O How Can I Be Blythe and Glad'), in Wilhelm Gerhard's German translation.
schumann-weit-weit.music: Simple and folk-like, with a lilting 6/8 and a little sigh on 'weit, weit'.

brahms-o-liebliche-wangen.story: O lovely cheeks, you make me long to see you, to greet you, to touch you, to kiss you. O fairest of the fair: come quickly, take my longing away, or I will die of it.
brahms-o-liebliche-wangen.poem: Words by Paul Fleming (1609-1640), a German Baroque poet.
brahms-o-liebliche-wangen.music: Fast and ardent, with a surging accompaniment that grows more urgent as he pleads.
